paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. Psalm 149 says praise is for the people God loves, and He loves them first. The psalm calls Israel to rejoice in their Maker and their King, and then it gives the reason: "For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He adorns the afflicted with salvation." (Ps 149:4) So the singing and dancing and tambourines don't come first. His pleasure in His people does.

That matters if you ever feel worn down, like a stamper with blurry edges in the back of a drawer. The psalm says He adorns the afflicted with salvation, and that's just what He did when He reached into my drawer. Your praise doesn't have to be polished, because it answers what He's already done. So sing the new song, even if you're shouting it from your bed. (Ps 149:1, 5)

Now, the sword part is heavy, and I won't pretend it isn't. The psalm pairs praise with judgment on the nations, and it says the judgment is "written against them." (Ps 149:6-9) The saints don't choose it for themselves, because it was written already. And the psalm ends where it began: "This honor is for all His saints. Hallelujah!" (Ps 149:9)
